idiom_name: hand-written recursive matcher over a tagged-union AST (node kind switch plus child recursion)
implementation_notes: C has no syntax-tree facility, so the classic structure is written by hand: an AST of structs with a kind tag and children, a matcher function per shape that destructures kind plus selected children, and a small engine that walks the tree and applies an ordered rule table of {match, action} pairs. When the subject is C source itself, libclang walks a cursor tree for you - clang_visitChildren with CXCursorVisitor over CXCursorKind, returning CXChildVisit_Recurse, Continue or Break - but that replaces the parser and the traversal only; the pattern/action rules stay hand-written, and tree-sitter queries are the other out-of-process option when the patterns should be data. Keep matching and walking apart: the matcher answers whether one node matches a shape, and the engine decides where and how often to try it.
pitfalls: Nothing is managed: a rewrite that replaces a node must free or hand back the old subtree deliberately, and an engine that walks while mutating leaks memory or dereferences freed nodes.
There is no exhaustiveness checking: a matcher that forgets a node kind simply returns false and the rule never fires, so every pattern needs a fixture with the exact shape it targets.
Recursion depth follows tree depth, so deeply nested input (generated expressions, fuzzed parser output) overflows the stack unless the engine keeps an explicit worklist instead of recursing.
